answer.exemplar: A correlation is a report that two quantities moved together across the group that was observed, and it says nothing whatever about why. In a study of revision hours against exam score, a coefficient of 0.92 delivers two claims and no more: students who revised more tended to score higher, and the relationship is a strong one in the sense that the line tracks the data closely. Three things follow from the fact that the design was observational. The direction is not established, because students who expect to do well may revise more, and the causation may run the other way, or both may follow from a third thing. Confounders are the serious problem, since prior attainment, motivation, and home support all plausibly raise both revision and score, and a coefficient computed on the raw data cannot separate revision from whatever travels alongside it. The strength does not rescue the claim either, because a very strong correlation can be entirely produced by a confounder, and 0.92 makes the error look smaller rather than larger. To support a causal claim the design has to change: assign revision hours deliberately, which fixes direction and balances the confounders across groups, or hold motivation and prior attainment fixed and compare like with like. Failing that, the honest statement is the correlational one, and it is not a weak claim, merely a different one.

questions.explanation: A good answer separates what the coefficient delivers, which is a strong tendency across the observed group, from what it cannot deliver, which is any statement about mechanism. The confounders have to be named, since prior attainment and motivation are the obvious ones, and the point that strength does not help is worth making because 0.92 feels like a warranty. The remedy is a design change, random assignment or matching on prior attainment, not a larger sample of the same observational data.
questions.hint: Separate the claim the data delivers from the claim the reader wants, then say what design would be needed.
questions.learningObjective: explain why a correlation does not establish causation and what would be needed

answer.exemplar: A box plot is a picture of where the data sits along one axis, drawn from five numbers. The two ends of the whiskers are the minimum and the maximum, the two ends of the box are the lower and upper quartiles, and the line inside the box is the median, so the middle half of the data fills the box and the median splits it into equal halves. The quartiles are positions in the ordering rather than measurements of the data, which is why a box plot of a given set is not unique: conventions differ over how the quartiles are located when the count is not a multiple of four, and two box plots of identical data can differ slightly as a result. The display is strong precisely because it makes shape and spread visible at a glance, and two box plots can be compared without any arithmetic. It is equally clear about what it withholds, since every reading between the quartiles and between the whisker and the box has been summarised away, so the number of readings in each region is invisible, and a gap in the data or a second cluster will not show up unless it lies outside the whiskers. A box plot is therefore a statement about the shape of a distribution, not a substitute for the readings themselves.

questions.explanation: The answer should name the five values and be explicit that the box holds the middle half, since that is what the width measures. The strengths are worth stating: two distributions can be compared visually with no arithmetic, and shape shows at once. The limitations are the substance of the second half, because everything between the marked positions has been summarised away, so counts, gaps, and internal clusters are all invisible, and the convention for locating quartiles should be mentioned since it is a genuine source of variation between displays.
questions.hint: Say what the five marked positions are, then say what the picture cannot show.
questions.learningObjective: explain what a box plot shows and what it hides

answer.exemplar: The margin of error and bias answer two different questions, and keeping them apart is the whole point. A margin of error measures how much a fair sample's answer typically wanders from the population's true answer, and it shrinks as the square root of the sample size, so going from 400 to 4000 respondents halves the band and no more. That shrinkage is conditional on the sample being fair, and a fair sample means every member of the population had a known chance of selection, which is why random selection matters rather than merely many people. Bias is the systematic difference between what the sample reports and what the population holds, and it comes entirely from the selection mechanism: a poll taken in one supermarket, or among the callers to a telephone line, is a better description of that supermarket and of those callers than of the country. Enlarging such a sample makes the bias more precisely measured rather than smaller, so a poll of 2000 people drawn from one forum can be wrong by 18 percentage points while reporting a margin of error of only 2. The practical consequence is that a margin of error attached to a biased figure is close to worthless, since it measures the precision of a wrong answer. A responsible report therefore has to supply both, and when the two cannot both be had, the honest course is to say which is missing.

questions.explanation: A strong answer makes the two questions explicit, because precision is about the sample and bias is about the selection, and neither substitutes for the other. The key practical point is that size only tightens the band, so a large biased poll is a precisely wrong answer, and the example of a figure of 70 against a truth of 52 with a narrow band makes that concrete. The conclusion to reach is that a margin of error only means something alongside a stated random selection method.
questions.hint: Ask separately what the band measures and what the selection method measures.
questions.learningObjective: explain why a smaller margin of error does not remove bias

answer.exemplar: A residual plot shows, for every data point, how far it sits from the line of best fit, with the vertical axis carrying the residual and the horizontal axis the value of x. Because least squares chooses a line to make the residuals small, and because a fitted line is free to slide and tilt, two properties come for free: the residuals total zero, and the line passes through the mean of both variables. What the plot adds is the pattern those two totals cannot reveal, since a set of residuals can sum to zero while being arranged in any pattern at all. A cloud with no structure is what a straight line is entitled to produce, and it is the picture that licenses reading the relationship as linear. A curve is the clearest violation, since the line cuts the middle and the points sit alternately above and below in a sweep, which says the relationship bends and a different model is needed. Points that fan out, with the spread of the residuals growing as x increases, break a different assumption, since the same vertical error is being predicted more tightly at one end than at the other, and a run of residuals of one sign in a stretch of x points to something the line has missed locally. A single point far from the band stands out as a possible outlier, which is a reason to investigate the reading rather than to delete it, since the pattern says where to look and not what the answer is.

questions.explanation: The answer should say what is plotted on each axis and then treat the pattern as the content of the display, since the totals summing to zero tell the reader nothing about shape. The curved pattern is the one to describe in detail, with points above the line at one end and below at the other, because it is the strongest evidence against a linear model. Fanning and sign runs are worth adding, and the closing point is that a residual plot points at where to investigate rather than supplying the answer itself.
questions.hint: Say what the two axes carry, then name the patterns that a straight line cannot produce.
questions.learningObjective: explain what a residual plot reveals about a model's assumptions
